results.headline: Huawei drives China's push to make its own advanced chips

chunks.text:
Lithography remains one of the biggest obstacles to China's push for semiconductor self-sufficiency. Local chipmakers still rely heavily on the Netherlands' ASML for the equipment needed to manufacture advanced semiconductors, while domestic alternatives lag on critical components including projection lenses and high-powered light sources.
Huawei is seeking to close those gaps by backing local suppliers and helping push their equipment into commercial fabs, where years of testing and refinement are needed before domestic machines can compete with established foreign equipment. Success would also leave China less vulnerable to western export controls.
"Huawei is playing a project management role in China's DUV push," said Lin Qingyuan, a semiconductor analyst at Bernstein. "Simply having a DUV prototype is not enough. You need thousands of vendors and customers to work together to push it forward and a central orchestrating power to bring this effort together."

Another major bottleneck in China's attempt to develop domestic lithography equipment is the light source. Japanese supplier Gigaphoton and ASML subsidiary Cymer are the dominant suppliers.
"This is a key technical hurdle for China," said Bernstein's Lin. "Building a light source is easy, but having one that works very stably at such high power is difficult."
Multiple industry executives pointed to progress by Beijing RSLaser Opto-Electronics, a leading developer of the type of light source used in DUV. RSLaser has also received investment from Huawei's Habo.
RSLaser has supplied light sources for older-generation DUV equipment made by Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment, according to public disclosures. RSLaser is also working with SMEE on the light source for its 28nm DUV machine, Chinese media have reported.

With the support of Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment, a longstanding local lithography manufacturer, Yuliangsheng is developing multiple DUV prototypes. Some rely on critical foreign components, while others are testing local alternatives.
DUV machines contain tens of thousands of parts across roughly a dozen major component groups. Chinese suppliers lag behind foreign rivals in two of the most complex: projection lenses and light sources.
Huawei's corporate venture arm Habo, which invests in areas where China relies on foreign technology, and another Huawei-backed fund, Shenzhen Yuanzhi Xinghuo, have both backed suppliers targeting critical equipment bottlenecks.
Yuliangsheng uses projection lenses made by Germany's Zeiss for its DUV machines, according to two people familiar with the matter. Zeiss said it only sold its lithography optics to ASML.

We are increasingly receiving orders for 2028 and customers are also expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030.

chunks.text:
The two also work together. In a joint release in September, ASML and TSMC said they had formed an initiative to move High NA EUV lithography to larger photomasks, and that TSMC intends to use ASML's High NA technology in high-volume manufacturing for advanced nodes starting in 2030.
Investors often compare them because their businesses are closely linked, even though their financial profiles differ.
The case for ASML
ASML supplies chipmakers with lithography systems and related software and services used to print circuit patterns on silicon wafers. Its flagship products include Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) and Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) machines used to produce advanced chips. ASML says it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems. According to ASML's 2025 annual report, four customers accounted for about 61% of ASML's 2025 net sales.

results.headline: TSMC, ASML Launch 12-inch EUV Mask Initiative

chunks.text:
02:35 AM EDT, 09/08/2026 (MT Newswires) -- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TPE:2330) and NASDAQ-listed ASML Holding have formed a collaborative industry initiative to drive the transition to larger-format 12-inch photomasks for EUV lithography.
In a joint statement on Tuesday, the two parties said they are targeting to establish a 12-inch mask pilot line by 2031, which will support full lithography system readiness for advanced node production by 2033.
The transition will increase fab productivity, lower chip-making costs, and remove stitching constraints.

Recent News
On Sept. 9, 2026, ASML announced a collaboration with Xanadu Quantum Technologies Limited to advance lithography processes for Xanadu's photonic quantum hardware. The partnership is aimed at exploring how advanced lithography innovations can reduce optical losses in quantum computing chips and support progress toward utility-scale quantum computing (USQC). The companies will evaluate lithography-enabled process approaches designed to improve patterning control and enable lower-loss photonic structures.
On Sept. 8, 2026, ASML and Samsung Electronics expanded their long-standing strategic partnership, strengthening cooperation in High-NA EUV lithography and advanced semiconductor manufacturing technologies. The collaboration is intended to accelerate the development and deployment of next-generation technologies capable of meeting the rising performance and efficiency requirements of semiconductor manufacturing, particularly amid growing demand related to Al applications.

results.headline: ASML Has a China Warning for Trump: Too Much Pressure Could Create a Competitor

chunks.text:
"If you over-restrict, you bring desperation," Fouquet said, arguing that desperation could create a stronger incentive to build competing technology.
The concern is not entirely theoretical. Fouquet pointed to Huawei's emergence as a significant force in China's development of deep ultraviolet, or DUV, lithography technology.
Read Also: ASML's China Business Defies Chip War Fears
The Competitor Nobody Wants
That creates an unusual problem for ASML.
The company produces some of the most advanced EUV lithography machines. Reproducing that technology is enormously complex. ASML says its EUV machines involve more than 100,000 parts supplied through a network of 200 principal suppliers and roughly 2,000 companies.
The current export-control framework therefore limits China's access to a critical piece of the advanced-chip manufacturing chain.

results.headline: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations

chunks.text:
ASML sticks to China forecast
The semiconductor equipment maker said it expects China sales to account for 20% of its total business, sticking to a prior forecast.
While ASML holds an effective monopoly on EUV machines, a July report from The Information suggested an unnamed Chinese company had begun manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine, citing people familiar with the matter.
ASML dominates the manufacturing of DUV machines, which are less advanced than EUV. China has been ramping up its domestic semiconductor supply chain, with some investors concerned it could challenge the European and U.S. dominance. However, analysts raised questions about China's ability to ramp up its own DUV technology.
ASML meanwhile has faced challenges in China over the last few years. The company is restricted from selling EUV and some DUV tools to China.

Price increase negotiations completed; effects to be partially reflected in 2027 and fully realized from 2028
Price negotiations that began last quarter have been finalized. The increase targets high-spec bilateral pricing that provides the most value to customers, and upgrade pricing will also be adjusted in the same direction in linkage with long-term pricing. Due to lead times, the effect will not be seen in 2026, will be partially reflected in 2027, and will be fully reflected from 2028. While part of the increase is used for internal ramp-up costs and supply chain support following production increases, a significant portion contributes directly to gross margin. The CFO emphasized that this increase is not planned to be repeated annually, but was conducted within a framework of maintaining value-based pricing principles so as not to be exposed to price reduction pressure when the market slows down.

8. ASML Holding Shareholder Returns and Relative Stock Price Comparison
Valuation burden is not high when reflecting equipment profit growth, but caution is advised regarding volatility
Reflecting ASML's equipment profit growth, the valuation burden has eased to a level similar to its peers. ASML's 12MF P/E is 29.6x, which is higher than the Dutch market at 15.3x and the semiconductor industry at 20.3x. However, the PEG reflecting the 43.0% EPS CAGR for the next 3 years (2026–2028) is 0.7x, which is similar to peers Lam Research (0.7x) and Applied Materials (0.6x).
The drop in multiples compared to last quarter's P/E of 37.7x and PEG of 1.1x is due to the upward revision of EPS estimates (CAGR 33.0% -> 43.0%) outstripping the stock price increase; the high P/E is judged to be a premium supported by earnings growth.
The 12MF P/B is 17.3x, down from 20.6x last quarter, and ROE has improved from 53.7% to 56.9%, somewhat reducing the stock price burden relative to equity. However, EV/EBITDA of 23.2x and EV/Sales of 10.6x still significantly exceed the semiconductor industry averages of 14.7x and 7.8x, respectively, maintaining a qualitative premium.
Within peer companies, processor makers such as NVIDIA (PEG 0.2x) and Broadcom (PEG 0.3x) have lower multiples, limiting the relative valuation attractiveness of equipment makers. While the mid-to-long-term growth story remains valid, it is necessary to watch for increased short-term volatility.

Reasons To Buy:
Al and Lithography Intensity: As a leading provider of holistic lithography solutions, ASML is benefiting from a demand cycle that extends beyond a single node transition. In second- quarter 2026, management observed that Al-related demand is driving customers to add capacity across 5-, 4- and 3-nanometer Logic. Memory customers are also adding capacity as DDR and HBM demand remains elevated. Newer Logic and DRAM nodes require more EUV and advanced immersion exposures, raising lithography intensity alongside wafer capacity. Management expects 2026 advanced foundry Logic revenue to increase about 25% and Memory revenue to rise 75%. It also expects EUV revenues to grow about 45% and DUV, metrology and inspection revenues to increase about 25%. This combination of capacity growth and higher lithography content gives ASML multiple structural avenues for revenue expansion through 2026 and beyond.

Summary
Price, Consensus & Surprise(1)
ASML's investment case balances favorable demand visibility against execution and policy risks. Al-driven investment is lifting advanced Logic and Memory capacity needs, while rising lithography intensity supports EUV, DUV and installed- base demand. Customer commitments extend into later years, and High-NA adoption adds another path for technology leadership. Profitability also benefits from increased upgrades, higher volumes and an improved systems mix. Offsetting these positives, growth depends on customers sustaining elevated capital spending and on ASML expanding output without disrupting costs or supply. China remains a material market, leaving results exposed to export- control uncertainty. High-NA has entered production, but broader customer insertion timing is not yet settled. These offsetting factors support a Neutral view.

Al-led capacity investment, rising lithography intensity, deeper order visibility, expanding services and High-NA adoption support ASML's durable long-term growth prospects.
Order Visibility Supports Capacity Plan: Current customer commitments provide ASML with longer demand visibility than projected earlier in 2026. By second-quarter 2026, the company was reportedly close to receiving all EUV orders needed for 2027 and had already received a large number of EUV orders for 2028. ASML plans to raise low-NA EUV capacity by about 30% in 2027 from roughly 65 systems in 2026 and is exploring another 30% increase for 2028. DUV immersion capacity is following the same path from a 2026 base of about 130 systems. The order profile reduces reliance on near-term bookings alone and supports a multi-year production ramp. Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to EUR43-EUR45 billion and gross margin guidance to 54-56%, while third-quarter 2026 sales are expected at EUR11-EUR12 billion.

The most consequential fact about EUV lithography in China is a negative one: not a single machine has ever crossed its borders. Under American pressure starting as early as 2018, the Netherlands withheld ASML's export license for EUV in 2019 and has never granted one since. The cutting edge of lithography was closed to China before the technology's centrality to artificial intelligence was fully apparent-in what remains arguably the single most important intervention in the architecture of Western technology controls.
The restrictions did not stop there. Instead, they steadily ratcheted, operating through case-by-case licensing rather than outright prohibition. In June 2023, the Dutch introduced national export controls requiring a government license to ship the most advanced immersion DUV systems-the tier directly below EUV, and the very tools on which China's most sophisticated production depends. Though framed as country-neutral, naming neither China nor ASML, the measure's effect was unequivocal: ASML promptly instructed its Chinese customers not to expect shipment approvals after January 1, 2024. The cutting edge of lithography was closed to China before the technology's centrality to artificial intelligence was fully apparent-in what remains arguably the single most important intervention in the architecture of Western technology controls.

results.headline: Alternatives Surmounting Monopoly Limits (ASML): Can China bypass EUV restrictions and keep up with Moore's law?

chunks.text:
Exclusion by licence
The most consequential fact about EUV lithography in China is a negative one: not a single machine has ever crossed its borders. Under American pressure starting as early as 2018, the Netherlands withheld ASML's export license for EUV in 2019 and has never granted one since. The cutting edge of lithography was closed to China before the technology's centrality to artificial intelligence was fully apparent-in what remains arguably the single most important intervention in the architecture of Western technology controls.
The restrictions did not stop there. Instead, they steadily ratcheted, operating through case-by-case licensing rather than outright prohibition. In June 2023, the Dutch introduced national export controls requiring a government license to ship the most advanced immersion DUV systems-the tier directly below EUV, and the very tools on which China's most sophisticated production depends. Though framed as country-neutral, naming neither China nor ASML, the measure's effect was unequivocal: ASML promptly instructed its Chinese customers not to expect shipment approvals after January 1, 2024. By September 2024, the licensing net widened to intermediate immersion models, and soon extended to the servicing, spare parts, and software support for restricted tools already installed-effectively shifting the battleground from the sale of new machines to the continued operation of existing ones9.

results.headline: Why Asia or the US have not produced a rival to ASML

chunks.text:
As a result, chipmakers are unwilling to experiment with unproven EUV tools in volume production. That means a rival would never accumulate the field data required to improve. ASML shipped its first EUV machine in 2006 and its first production capable system in 2013. Because chip factories run around the clock, cumulative operating hours now run into the millions. That gap in real world operating data explains why Nikon and Canon, once ASML's peers in lithography, ultimately withdrew from pursuing EUV lithography systems over a decade before it became commercially viable, and why no successor has emerged since their exit.
Governments are often proposed as the solution. In theory, a determined state, backed by subsidies and guaranteed local buyers, could create a rival. China is one example. It has treated chipmaking as a national priority since export controls cut Huawei off from advanced chips in 2020. Efforts to make its own chipmaking machines are ongoing and heavily funded.
Yet China's experience so far has been the strongest test of the idea that money and policy can create a rival. ASML shows how, beyond a certain technological threshold, markets no longer correct monopolies.

The 2022 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management prescribes a benchmark that will only be conducted for the TCC level - from which the base salary of Board of Management members is derived. ASML's values of challenge, collaborate and care sit front and center in everything that the Remuneration Committee does. We challenge ourselves about all aspects of remuneration and collaborate with colleagues within ASML as well as external experts and advisers. Our aim is to arrive at fair and balanced decisions that drive long-term performance.
2024 performance
In 2024, ASML performed very well on the metrics that are part of the Board of Management's incentive plans. For the short-term incentive (STI), performance was between target and stretch for all performance measures - EBIT Margin %, Customer Orientation and Technology Leadership Index - resulting in an overall pay-out of 136.1% of target. For the long-term incentive (LTI) 2022-2024 series, ASML exceeded target on most the performance metrics - Relative Total Shareholder Return (rTSR), Cash Conversion Rate, Technology Leadership Index and ESG. The overall LTI result is a vesting of 132.3% of target.

Hereby, the Strategic Orientation measures align with key business priorities that are critical to achieving our strategic objectives. If the proposed 2025 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management is not adopted by the 2025 AGM, performance measure Strategic Orientation will be replaced with the Technology Leadership Index in line with the current Remuneration Policy.
Corporate governance Supervisory Board report Remuneration report

Board of Management remuneration (continued)
Explanation of changes in company's performance versus remuneration
The foregoing table aims to provide insight into our performance over the past five years and the development of the remuneration. The metrics net sales, net income and share price are used to measure performance, as they are key metrics serving as a good proxy for our general performance, as well as in view of comparability with other companies. Actual remuneration may fluctuate year-on-year depending on actual STI pay-out in any year, as well as the vesting of performance shares (LTI) in any year and the share price at that moment.
We have grown significantly over recent years, which is not only reflected in the number of employees but also in terms of performance. Over the last five years, net sales increased by 202%, net income increased by 218% based on US GAAP (226% based on EU-IFRS) and ASML's share price increased by more than 170%. This shows that our performance has improved significantly, leading to several revisions of the Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management in past years (last update in 2022), resulting in higher base salaries as well as higher target levels of STI and LTI leading to a similar increase in the remuneration over this same period.

Board of Management remuneration (continued)
Total direct compensation
The remuneration levels are determined using the Total Cash Compensation (TCC). TCC consists of base salary and STI. TCC together with LTI constitutes total direct compensation.
Base salary
The 2022 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management prescribes a benchmark that will only be conducted for the TCC level - from which the base salary of Board of Management members is derived. The actual base salary and annual increases will be reported in the Remuneration Report. The base salary for the Board of Management for the reporting year 2024 is disclosed in the table Total remuneration Board of Management.
Variable compensation
The variable compensation consists of the STI and the LTI. The performance metrics are set by the Supervisory Board and consist of financial and non-financial metrics in such a way that an optimal balance is achieved between the various company objectives, both in the short and the long term. By doing so, we ensure the variable compensation contributes to our strategy, long-term interests and sustainability. The Supervisory Board may adjust the performance metrics and their relative weighting of the variable income based on the rules and principles as outlined in the 2022 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management of ASML Holding NV, if required by changed strategic priorities in any given year. The Supervisory Board assesses the extent to which performance metrics are met at the end of a performance period.

Short-term incentive 2024
The financial and non-financial target levels for the STI were set at the beginning of the 2024 financial year in accordance with the 2022 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management and taking into account the annual plan (forecast) for 2024.
For the STI, the Supervisory Board, taking into consideration our business challenges and circumstances in 2024, decided to select a performance metric focused on profitability:
- EBIT Margin %, measuring Income from operations as percentage of total net sales (based on US GAAP).
In addition, the following non-financial performance metrics applied for the STI in 2024, in accordance with the Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management:
- Customer Orientation: This metric consisted of five sub-targets measuring ASML's positioning in the market and its performance in terms of customer experience, customer satisfaction and quality.

Main responsibilities
- Overseeing the development and implementation of the Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management and preparing the Supervisory Board Remuneration Policy
- Reviewing and proposing to the Supervisory Board corporate goals and objectives relevant to the variable part of the Board of Management's remuneration
- Carrying out scenario analyses of the possible financial outcomes on the variable remuneration of meeting these goals, as well as exceeding these goals, before proposing these corporate goals and objectives to the Supervisory Board for approval
- Evaluating the performance of the members of the Board of Management in view of those goals and objectives and - based on this evaluation - recommending to the Supervisory Board appropriate compensation levels for the members of the Board of Management
- Staying apprised of external pay practices and the effectiveness of our Remuneration Policy and incentive measures in attracting and retaining top talent

In addition to the Remuneration Committee members, the Remuneration Committee generally invites the CEO, the CFO, the Executive Vice President HR&O, and the Vice President Global Compensation and Benefits to attend its meetings. The Remuneration Committee's external adviser is also invited to attend the Remuneration Committee meetings when deemed necessary.

More indirectly, we want to ensure that our 2022 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management enables us to attract, motivate and retain qualified industry professionals for the Board of Management in order to define and achieve our strategic goals. This is reflected by our drive to determine a remuneration structure and remuneration levels that intend to be closer to competitive levels in the relevant labor market, while being aware of societal trends and perception. Therefore, the 2022 Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management acknowledges the internal and external context as well as our business needs and long-term strategy.
The Remuneration Policy for the Board of Management is designed to encourage behavior that is focused on long-term value creation and the long-term interests and sustainability of ASML, while adopting the highest standards of good corporate governance. It is aimed at motivating the Board of Management members to achieve outstanding results, using a combination of non-financial and financial performance measures as well as an appropriate ratio between base salary and variable compensation. Technology leadership, customer value creation and employee engagement are the key drivers of sustainable returns to our shareholders.

Target-setting process

ASML said it is investing EUR1.3 billion in Mistral AI's Series C funding round as lead investor. As a result, ASML will hold an 11% share in Mistral AI on a fully diluted basis.
Mistral is raising a total of EUR1.7 billion in the funding round, which will value the company at almost EUR12 billion."},{"cnum":2,"text":"The semiconductor company will gain a seat on Mistral AI's strategic committee as part of the investment, giving it an advisory role in future strategy and technology decisions.
ASML Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen will take on this role, in addition to his existing responsibilities.

"We believe that this strategic partnership with Mistral AI, which goes beyond a traditional vendor-client relationship, is the best way to capture this significant opportunity. We also believe that this collaboration is value enhancing to Mistral AI."
Arthur Mensch, Mistral AI's co-founder and CEO added: "We are proud to engage in this long-term partnership with ASML, combining our frontier AI expertise with ASML's unmatched industrial leadership and most sophisticated engineering capabilities. These assumptions involve estimation uncertainty and could result in a significant remeasurement of the carrying amount within the next financial period. results.headline: ASML invests EUR1.3 billion in French AI firm Mistral for 11% stake

chunks.text:
(Alliance News) - ASML Holding NV on Tuesday said it has agreed to invest EUR1.3 billion in French artificial intelligence firm Mistral AI SAS and has struck a long-term collaboration agreement.
The Veldhoven, Netherlands-based semiconductor manufacturer said the strategic partnership will also involve AI research, development and operations "to benefit ASML customers with faster time to market and higher performance holistic lithography systems".
ASML said it is investing EUR1.3 billion in Mistral AI's Series C funding round as lead investor. As a result, ASML will hold an 11% share in Mistral AI on a fully diluted basis.
Mistral is raising a total of EUR1.7 billion in the funding round, which will value the company at almost EUR12 billion.

The semiconductor company will gain a seat on Mistral AI's strategic committee as part of the investment, giving it an advisory role in future strategy and technology decisions.
ASML Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen will take on this role, in addition to his existing responsibilities.
"The collaboration between Mistral AI and ASML aims to generate clear benefits for ASML customers through innovative products and solutions enabled by AI, and will offer potential for joint research to address future opportunities," said ASML Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet.
"We believe that this strategic partnership with Mistral AI, which goes beyond a traditional vendor-client relationship, is the best way to capture this significant opportunity. We also believe that this collaboration is value enhancing to Mistral AI."
Arthur Mensch, Mistral AI's co-founder and CEO added: "We are proud to engage in this long-term partnership with ASML, combining our frontier AI expertise with ASML's unmatched industrial leadership and most sophisticated engineering capabilities. We believe this partnership will strengthen Mistral AI's proposition, position, and value in the AI market."
Shares in ASML were up 0.6% at EUR680.50 in Amsterdam on Tuesday morning.

The fair value of the equity investment in Mistral AI was determined using a venture capital valuation method. This method reflects Mistral AI's current stage of development and overall growth phase of the industry in which it operates, and incorporates assumptions such as expected market growth and related market share, range of peer companies revenue multiples, expected time to exit and venture capital target return. These assumptions involve estimation uncertainty and could result in a significant remeasurement of the carrying amount within the next financial period. The fair value of the equity investment increases (decreases) when expected market growth, market share, or peer companies' revenue multiples increase (decrease), and decreases (increases) when the venture capital target return or estimated time to exit increase (decrease). Multiple favorable or unfavorable changes may occur simultaneously, as these assumptions may be interrelated. Accordingly, simultaneous favorable changes could significantly magnify the fair value, whereas unfavorable changes across inputs could have a negative effect.

Under the venture capital valuation method, expected market growth and market share (applying a business expansion rate of approximately 60%, which reflects market consensus on AI sector growth rate together with Mistral AI's expected scaling trajectory), peer companies revenue multiples (range from 7.1 to 61.4 at the valuation date), and venture capital target return (range from 30% to 50%, which reflects the level of risk associated with growth- stage companies) are assumed to have a more than insignificant impact on the fair value of the equity investment and are therefore treated as key unobservable inputs. The fair value of the equity investment in Mistral AI as of June 28, 2026, remained consistent with the fair value as of December 31, 2025, with no unrealized fair value remeasurements recognized in other comprehensive income. Investments in money market funds (included in our cash and cash equivalents) have fair value measurements which are all based on quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities. Money market and investment funds qualify as available for sale securities. Due to the short-term nature and investment-grade credit ratings, the fair value is close to the carrying value. These money market funds can be called on a daily basis. Investments and redemptions in money market funds are managed on a daily basis. ASML does not have trading securities as of June 28, 2026. Our short-term investments consist of deposits with original maturities to the entity holding the investments longer than three months and one year or less at the date of acquisition with financial institutions that have investment-grade credit ratings.

chunks.text: Silicon Valley types might sniff the startup is now little more than a "system integrator", with a chunk of its revenue stemming from Palantir-style consulting deals rather than cutting-edge AI. The strategy is working. Mistral now has the support of ASML, Europe's most valuable tech company ($560 billion market cap), which makes the equipment nearly the entire tech world relies on to etch circuits into silicon chips using ultraviolet light. The Dutch-listed firm led a $2 billion round into Mistral in September and signed a deal to use Mistral's AI in its products and research. 18-## Technology: software
19-
20:Scope: application and infrastructure software sold as subscriptions, licenses, usage or transactions. Hardware and semiconductors have their own primer; consumer internet platforms sit in communication services. A figure marked "(verify)" is a judgment or dated: check it against the peer set and period before use.
21-
22-## How the sector makes money and the value drivers
23-
24-Software is a knowledge business in Mauboussin's terms: high upfront cost, low cost per extra unit, no direct link between sales and costs, and an advantage that is hard to protect without lock-in or network effects (Total Addressable Market, 2015, pp.20, 23). The value drivers:
25-
26-- Recurring revenue growth = new customers + expansion within existing customers + price, minus contraction and churn.
27-- Gross margin: hosting, support and services costs. Subscription gross margin is commonly 70 to 85 percent (verify); services run near break-even.
28-- Operating margin at scale: sales and marketing and R&D are the real investment, and both are expensed.
29-- Reinvestment: little tangible capital, so growth is funded through the income statement, not the balance sheet.
30-- Duration of advantage: switching costs (data, integration, training), network effects and de facto standards. These are the conditions under which returns can rise with scale rather than fade (roic-moat notes, Mauboussin 2014, pp.14-15).
31-
32-## The metrics that matter
33-
34-| Metric | Definition | Why it matters |
35-|---|---|---|
36-| ARR | Annualized value of active recurring contracts, excluding services and uncommitted usage | Base for growth and efficiency ratios; definitions differ by company |
37-| Net revenue retention (NRR) | (Starting ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) / starting ARR, over 12 months, same cohort | Growth from the installed base; above 100 percent means the base grows without new logos |
38-| Gross revenue retention (GRR) | (Starting ARR - contraction - churn) / starting ARR | Stickiness with expansion removed; the cleaner test of switching costs |
39-| Remaining performance obligations (RPO, cRPO) | Contracted revenue not yet recognized; current portion due within 12 months | Leads revenue; length of contracts changes it |
40-| Billings | Revenue + change in deferred revenue | Demand signal, distorted by billing terms |
41-| CAC payback | Sales and marketing cost to win a customer / (new ARR x gross margin), in months | Speed at which growth spending is recovered in cash |

118:## Technology: semiconductors and hardware
119-
120:Scope: chip designers (fabless), integrated manufacturers, foundries, memory, semiconductor equipment and materials, and hardware makers (computers, storage, networking and communications equipment, devices). A figure marked "(verify)" is a judgment or dated: check it against the peer set and period before use.
121-
122-## How the sector makes money and the value drivers
123-
124-These are physical businesses with heavy preproduction cost: fabs, process development and chip design are paid before the first unit ships. Value comes from:
125-
126-- **Volume x price x mix.** Unit demand from end markets (PCs, phones, data centers, autos, industrial), average selling price, and the mix of leading-edge against mature products.
127:- **Price declines and the learning curve.** Prices for a given level of performance fall every year. Measuring the Moat (2013) shows semiconductor prices falling about 8.6 percent a year in 2006-2011, the steepest of the fast-cycle examples quoted (verify). Profit depends on moving down the cost curve faster than price: the median product cuts unit cost about 20 percent for each doubling of cumulative output.
128-- **Utilization.** With most costs fixed, gross margin follows fab or factory loading. Changes in capacity utilization correlate about 0.60 with changes in operating margin across large companies (1967-2015).
129-- **Capital intensity and reinvestment.** Leading-edge capacity and tools are expensive and arrive in large blocks; fabless designers carry R&D but little fixed capital.
130-- **Product cycles and design wins.** A win in a customer's platform sets revenue for its life; a missed node or generation is hard to recover.
131-
132-## The metrics that matter
133-
134-| Metric | Definition | Why it matters |
135-|---|---|---|
136-| Book-to-bill | Orders / shipments in the period (equipment, some components) | Leads revenue by one to several quarters |
137-| Inventory days, company and channel | Inventory / cost of goods sold x 365; distributor and customer weeks of supply | Rising days ahead of a slowdown signal a correction |
138-| Utilization | Output / capacity | Drives gross margin through fixed-cost absorption |
139-| Gross margin | (Revenue - COGS) / revenue | Mix, pricing and utilization in one number |
78-
79-- **Banks.** No enterprise DCF and no net debt: interest is operating. Value cash flow to equity at the cost of equity, CFE = net income - increase in book equity + other comprehensive income, with equity growth set by the capital ratio (Tier 1 or CET1 on risk-weighted assets). CV = NI(t+1) x (1 - g / RONE) / (ke - g); if RONE = ROE, P/B = (ROE - g) / (ke - g), so P/B above 1 needs ROE above ke. Let ke move with leverage and asset mix. Model through-the-cycle loan losses by category and test reserve adequacy. Forecast margins from forward rates. Split net interest income into economic spread, maturity-mismatch and matched-maturity charges; a one-point change in loan rates moved the book's example bank's ROE by about 12 points (McKinsey ch. 36). Use scenarios.
80:- **Cyclicals.** Perfect-foresight DCF values are nearly flat while cash flows swing; consensus tends to ignore the cycle. Build a normal-cycle scenario with CV on mid-cycle profit and ROIC and a new-trend scenario extrapolating recent results, give each an economic rationale (demand, capacity, entry and exit), and weight them. Market prices fit a 50/50 blend of perfect and zero foresight (McKinsey ch. 35).
81-- **High growth** (organic revenue growth above 15 percent a year). Begin with the future: size the addressable market, cap share using an early saturated market, set long-run margin and capital intensity from mature analogues, work back to today and weight scenarios. Compare the revenue ramp with the median, not the mean, of analogues; negative invested capital makes ROIC meaningless and expensed marketing and technology overstate early returns (McKinsey ch. 34). The book's example weights three scenarios 20/50/30 for an expected $751m; calibrate weights to growth base rates.
82-- **Emerging markets.** Primary: scenario DCF with at least a business-as-usual and a crisis case at a global-investor cost of capital with no country premium. A country premium applies only to promised cash flows, never to probability-weighted ones: mixing double counts risk. Local risk-free = (1 + US rf) x (1 + local inflation) / (1 + US inflation) - 1 (1.04 x 1.048 / 1.001 - 1 = 8.9 percent for Brazil, 2009). Global beta and premium; cost of debt = dollar rf + systematic spread + inflation differential. Triangulate with multiples, since prices are weaker anchors (McKinsey ch. 33). Twenty emerging economies saw a real GDP fall above 5 percent about once every five years (book period, verify).
83-- **Multi-business companies.** Value each unit on its own ROIC, growth and WACC (peer unlevered beta relevered to the unit's structure); eliminate intercompany sales; value corporate costs as a negative unit; reconcile unit NOPAT and capital to the consolidated totals. A blended multiple matches none of the units (ConsumerCo: 8.5x, 5.9x and 11.2x units, 8.8x combined). Sum of the parts is valid only with peers of similar performance (McKinsey ch. 13, 19).
84-- **Distressed.** Do not deduct the market value of debt. For each scenario, equity = max(EV - face value of claims, 0), then weight: EV of 1,500 or 900 at 50/50 against debt of 1,200 gives equity of 150 (McKinsey ch. 12).
85-- **Inflation and currency.** Inflation in the cash flows matches inflation in the discount rate; translation gains are not cash flow; never use the parent's WACC for a subsidiary's local-currency cash flows (McKinsey ch. 29-30).
86-
87-## Interpretation and limits
88-
89-- A large terminal share does not mean value arises after the forecast; check value by business component and economic profit (McKinsey ch. 10).
90-- RONIC = WACC is not a default haircut, and RONIC above WACC needs modest growth. Uncertainty belongs in scenarios, not in a higher discount rate or a haircut (McKinsey ch. 2, 10).
91-- Exit multiples taken from today's market or a deal are circular (McKinsey ch. 10).
92-- Not in the sources: a procedure for RSUs and stock compensation beyond the two effects named (DCF II, p. 17). State the treatment and do not count an award both as an expense in FCF and in the share count.
3:This method answers: how does a forecast of growth, margin or return on capital compare with what actually happened to similar large companies, and how fast should an unusual level move back toward its sector mean. It starts from the history of a reference class (the outside view) and moves away from it only with evidence, instead of extrapolating the company's own story (the inside view). The inside view is usually too optimistic and its ranges too narrow (Base Rate Book, 2016). Every number in this file is a historical base rate for large, mostly listed companies. None is a forecast or a current fact.

6-

24:2. **Choose the reference class.** Size class by prior-year sales for growth; sector for margins, gross profitability and returns on capital; the above-$50B class for mega caps. The class must be large enough to be robust and narrow enough to be relevant. Done when the class, its N and its label are stated. If the company differs in a way that matters, say which feature differs and still show the base rate.
25-3. **Read the distribution, not only the average.** Growth distributions are right-skewed: the median sits below the mean. Done when median, mean, dispersion and the relevant tail shares are quoted.
26-4. **Place the forecast in the distribution.** "Consensus needs a 10-year real sales CAGR of X percent, which Y percent of companies in the $A to $B class achieved." The tables give shares at fixed thresholds only; interpolate between them and say so. Not in the sources: full percentile tables.
27-5. **Convert real to nominal** before comparing with consensus (formula 4). Done when the inflation assumption is stated.
28:6. **Blend by persistence** (formula 1). Beyond three years, put the majority of the weight on the class median for sales and earnings growth. For margins and gross profitability, start from the latest level and fade toward the sector mean. For returns on capital, apply the horizon-matched r. Done when the blend, the weights and the r used are shown.
29-7. **Set a range at least as wide as history** and include a decline case (table 12). Done when the bear case includes shrinking real sales or lower net income.
30-8. **Ask what must be true for the price** (`references/expectations.md`) and whether that assumption sits in a rare part of the distribution. Claim an exception only with a specific, evidenced reason. Done when the note says how rare the implied path is.

22-## How the sector makes money and the value drivers
23-
24-Software is a knowledge business in Mauboussin's terms: high upfront cost, low cost per extra unit, no direct link between sales and costs, and an advantage that is hard to protect without lock-in or network effects (Total Addressable Market, 2015, pp.20, 23). The value drivers:
25-
26-- Recurring revenue growth = new customers + expansion within existing customers + price, minus contraction and churn.
27-- Gross margin: hosting, support and services costs. Subscription gross margin is commonly 70 to 85 percent (verify); services run near break-even.
28-- Operating margin at scale: sales and marketing and R&D are the real investment, and both are expensed.
29-- Reinvestment: little tangible capital, so growth is funded through the income statement, not the balance sheet.
30-- Duration of advantage: switching costs (data, integration, training), network effects and de facto standards. These are the conditions under which returns can rise with scale rather than fade (roic-moat notes, Mauboussin 2014, pp.14-15).

40-| Billings | Revenue + change in deferred revenue | Demand signal, distorted by billing terms |

Local risk-free = (1 + US rf) x (1 + local inflation) / (1 + US inflation) - 1 (1.04 x 1.048 / 1.001 - 1 = 8.9 percent for Brazil, 2009). Global beta and premium; cost of debt = dollar rf + systematic spread + inflation differential. Triangulate with multiples, since prices are weaker anchors (McKinsey ch. 33). Twenty emerging economies saw a real GDP fall above 5 percent about once every five years (book period, verify).
83-- **Multi-business companies.** Value each unit on its own ROIC, growth and WACC (peer unlevered beta relevered to the unit's structure); eliminate intercompany sales; value corporate costs as a negative unit; reconcile unit NOPAT and capital to the consolidated totals. A blended multiple matches none of the units (ConsumerCo: 8.5x, 5.9x and 11.2x units, 8.8x combined). Sum of the parts is valid only with peers of similar performance (McKinsey ch. 13, 19).
84-- **Distressed.** Do not deduct the market value of debt. For each scenario, equity = max(EV - face value of claims, 0), then weight: EV of 1,500 or 900 at 50/50 against debt of 1,200 gives equity of 150 (McKinsey ch. 12).
85-- **Inflation and currency.** Inflation in the cash flows matches inflation in the discount rate; translation gains are not cash flow; never use the parent's WACC for a subsidiary's local-currency cash flows (McKinsey ch. 29-30).
86-
87-## Interpretation and limits
88-
89-- A large terminal share does not mean value arises after the forecast; check value by business component and economic profit (McKinsey ch. 10).
90-- RONIC = WACC is not a default haircut, and RONIC above WACC needs modest growth. Uncertainty belongs in scenarios, not in a higher discount rate or a haircut (McKinsey ch. 2, 10).
91-- Exit multiples taken from today's market or a deal are circular (McKinsey ch. 10).
92-- Not in the sources: a procedure for RSUs and stock compensation beyond the two effects named (DCF II, p. 17). State the treatment and do not count an award both as an expense in FCF and in the share count.
3:This method answers: how does a forecast of growth, margin or return on capital compare with what actually happened to similar large companies, and how fast should an unusual level move back toward its sector mean. It starts from the history of a reference class (the outside view) and moves away from it only with evidence, instead of extrapolating the company's own story (the inside view). The inside view is usually too optimistic and its ranges too narrow (Base Rate Book, 2016). Every number in this file is a historical base rate for large, mostly listed companies. None is a forecast or a current fact.
4-
5-## When a skill loads this file
6-
7-Load it next to any growth, margin or return claim: earnings preview, valuation, thesis, deep dive, moat, scenarios, sector work. For a narrow question ("how often do companies this size grow 20 percent a year?") quote the relevant row with its label and stop.
8-
9-## Inputs
--
19:| Sector mean and persistence r | Tables below | reported (historical base rate) |
20-
21-## Procedure
22-
23-1. **State the quantity and the horizon.** Real or nominal growth, margin or return on capital, over how many years. Done when both are written.
24:2. **Choose the reference class.** Size class by prior-year sales for growth; sector for margins, gross profitability and returns on capital; the above-$50B class for mega caps. The class must be large enough to be robust and narrow enough to be relevant. Done when the class, its N and its label are stated. If the company differs in a way that matters, say which feature differs and still show the base rate.
25-3. **Read the distribution, not only the average.** Growth distributions are right-skewed: the median sits below the mean. Done when median, mean, dispersion and the relevant tail shares are quoted.
26-4. **Place the forecast in the distribution.** "Consensus needs a 10-year real sales CAGR of X percent, which Y percent of companies in the $A to $B class achieved." The tables give shares at fixed thresholds only; interpolate between them and say so. Not in the sources: full percentile tables.
27-5. **Convert real to nominal** before comparing with consensus (formula 4). Done when the inflation assumption is stated.
28:6. **Blend by persistence** (formula 1). Beyond three years, put the majority of the weight on the class median for sales and earnings growth. For margins and gross profitability, start from the latest level and fade toward the sector mean. For returns on capital, apply the horizon-matched r. Done when the blend, the weights and the r used are shown.
29-7. **Set a range at least as wide as history** and include a decline case (table 12). Done when the bear case includes shrinking real sales or lower net income.
30-8. **Ask what must be true for the price** (`references/expectations.md`) and whether that assumption sits in a rare part of the distribution. Claim an exception only with a specific, evidenced reason. Done when the note says how rare the implied path is.
31-

33-
34-**1. Regression to the mean and shrinkage** (Mauboussin, "How to Model Reversion to the Mean", 2013, "F"; Base Rate Book, 2016, "A")

47-**3. Threshold margin** (A)
48-
49-Incremental threshold margin = (incremental fixed capital rate + incremental working capital rate) x cost of capital / [(1 + cost of capital) x (1 - tax rate)]. Source example: (0.35 + 0.25) x 0.10 / (1.10 x 0.65) = 8.4 percent. Growth at that margin is value-neutral; growth below it destroys value.

content.text:
I've finished the ASML deep dive. It uses Bigdata.com data (company financials, consensus estimates, peer data, earnings-call transcripts, filings, broker notes and news) and five years of financial statements, because the data tool only returned five.

# ASML Holding (ASML): deep dive, 23 Oct 2026

Data as of: share price $1,589.60, the Oct 22, 2026 close in the Bigdata.com company data (about €1,419 at EUR/USD 1.12 on Oct 23); consensus estimates retrieved Oct 23, 2026 (FactSet, quarterly, number of estimates not given); statements FY2025 annual and Q3 2026 quarterly; newest document Oct 23, 2026.

## Summary

ASML is the only company that makes EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines, the tools needed to print the most advanced chips. It also leads the older DUV (deep ultraviolet) segment, and it services an installed base of machines that grows every year. FY2026 sales are guided to €44–45bn, about 36% growth [1].

The economics are exceptional, partly because customers pay large down payments that fund ASML's working capital:
- Return on invested capital (ROIC) was 123% in 2025 on capital net of cash and those prepayments (derived).
- Counting the prepayments as capital, ROIC was 42% (derived), against an assumed 9% cost of capital.

The competitive position rests on a sole-source EUV position that nobody has matched. Nikon left EUV in 2011 [27], and China's EUV prototype has not yet produced a working chip [23]. Pricing power is visible: ASML completed price increases on its most critical products that take effect from 2027 and fully from 2028 [1].

Earnings are mostly clean, with three caveats:
- Q3 2026 net income includes a €0.5bn revaluation gain on the Mistral AI stake [1].
- Gross margin is being lifted by machine-upgrade sales, which the CFO calls a "swing factor" [1].
- Operating cash flow depends on customer down payments, which reversed in 2023.

Capital allocation leans heavily to shareholders: 65% of 2021–2025 operating cash flow went to buybacks and dividends (derived). At today's price, the 2022–2025 buybacks returned roughly 2.5 times their cost (derived, approximate).

At an assumed 9% cost of capital, the price assumes consensus through 2028, then about 10% annual growth for another ten years at a 45% operating margin (derived). The probability-weighted value from three cases is about €1,005 per share at 9% (derived), with a range of €884–1,359 across 8–10% discount rates and terminal assumptions, below the €1,419 price. Peer multiples point the other way, to about €1,900. Most of that gap comes from the discount rate and from how long the advantage is assumed to last.

The main risk is a semiconductor capex cycle that turns after the AI build-out, combined with US legislation (the MATCH Act) that would ban DUV immersion sales and servicing in China. The next dated events are Nov 10, 2026, when the US Affiliates Rule suspension and China's rare-earth export-curb suspension both expire [8], and the Q4 results with 2027 guidance in January–February 2027.

## The business

ASML sells lithography systems (EUV, DUV immersion, DUV dry), metrology and inspection tools, and "Installed Base Management": service and upgrades on machines already in customer fabs. The Bigdata.com revenue segmentation section came back empty, so the segment figures below come from company calls.

| Segment | FY2025 | Growth 2025 | FY2026 guide (Oct 14) | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EUV systems | €11.6bn (48 systems incl. High-NA) | +39% | more than +45%; about 65 Low-NA units vs 44 | reported | [4], [1] |
| DUV systems | €12.0bn | -6% | non-EUV systems about +20% | reported | [4], [1] |
| Metrology and inspection | €0.83bn | +28% | YieldStar demand to more than double vs 2025 | reported | [4], [1] |
| Installed Base Management | €8.2bn | +26% | about +50% | reported | [4], [1] |
| Total net sales | €32.7bn | +16% | €44–45bn, gross margin about 56% | reported | [5], [1] |
| Logic / memory systems | €16.1bn / €8.4bn | +22% / -2% | about +10% (advanced logic more than +25%) / about +75% | reported | [4], [1] |

| Geography, share of net sales | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 guide | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| China | n/a | 36.1% | 29.1% | about 20% | reported | [7], [9], [1] |
| Taiwan | 29.3% | 15.4% | n/a | n/a | reported | [7] |
| South Korea | 25.2% | 22.7% | n/a | n/a | reported | [7] |
| Top four customers | n/a | n/a | about 61% | n/a | reported | [10] |

| Five-year trend (FactSet) | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue, €bn | 18.6 | 21.2 | 27.6 | 28.3 | 32.7 | reported |
| Gross margin | 51.9% | 49.5% | 50.2% | 49.8% | 51.6% | derived |
| R&D, % of sales | 13.1% | 14.5% | 13.5% | 13.9% | 13.2% | derived |
| Operating (EBIT) margin | 35.1% | 30.7% | 32.8% | 31.9% | 34.6% | derived |

Notes on the tables:
- Margins are FactSet line items over revenue. FactSet's 51.6% 2025 gross margin is below the company's 52.8% [5] because of how cost of sales is defined.
- Profit has shifted toward EUV and the installed base. The installed base was 25% of 2025 sales (derived) and carries "very high-margin" upgrade components [1].
- Q3 2026 gross margin was 57.5%. At the start of 2026 the company guided 51–53% [17].
- Backlog at end-2025 was €38.8bn, of which €25.5bn was EUV [5]. ASML no longer discloses bookings, and the CFO pointed to down payments in non-current liabilities as "a nice proxy" [1].

## Economics

ROIC is shown three ways because customer prepayments (€16.0bn of deferred revenue at end-2025) are larger than ASML's whole net operating capital. The report quotes the hand-built ROIC with goodwill and shows the version that counts prepayments as capital beside it.

| Year | Tax rate | NOPAT, €bn | Invested capital, €bn | ROIC (avg capital) | NOPAT margin x turnover | ROIC counting prepayments as capital | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 15.2% | 5.54 | 5.97 | 92.9% (year-end) | 29.8% x 3.12 | 39.9% | derived |
| 2022 | 15.0% | 5.52 | 4.61 | 104.5% | 26.1% x 4.01 | 35.7% | derived |
| 2023 | 15.8% | 7.61 | 9.38 | 108.9% | 27.6% x 3.94 | 40.2% | derived |
| 2024 | 18.6% | 7.35 | 8.05 | 84.3% | 26.0% x 3.24 | 35.4% | derived |
| 2025 | 17.7% | 9.31 | 7.12 | 122.7% | 28.5% x 4.31 | 42.5% | derived |

How the figures are built:
- NOPAT (net operating profit after tax) is EBIT times (1 minus the effective tax rate).
- Invested capital is equity plus debt minus cash and short-term investments minus long-term investments. The operating-side build (assets minus cash and investments, minus non-debt liabilities) gives the same figure.
- Excluding goodwill and intangibles, invested capital is negative in every year, so that version of ROIC has no meaning.
- Return on incremental invested capital (ROIIC) for 2022–2025 was 110% (change in NOPAT over the lagged change in capital, derived).
- The spread over an assumed 9% cost of capital is about 114 points on the quoted basis and about 34 points counting prepayments.
- Reconciliation with FactSet: FactSet's ROIC was 47.4% for FY2025 and 66.6% on a trailing basis at Q3 2026. It divides by total capital (equity plus debt, €24.3bn) without deducting the €13.3bn of cash and €3.8bn of investments.
- R&D is expensed under US GAAP. Capitalizing it would lower every ROIC figure, and the R&D history needed to do that is not in the data.
- Only five years are tabled because the tearsheet returns five fiscal periods and offers no period offset.

## Industry structure and moat

| Checklist item | Evidence | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Industry map and share | Sole commercial EUV supplier; JPMorgan put ASML's lithography share at 100% in 2023. In 2009 ASML had 65–70% value share against Nikon and Canon. | [29], [30] |
| Share stability | Share has risen over 15 years. Nikon and Canon withdrew from EUV more than a decade before it became commercially viable. | [36], [27] |
| Pricing power | Price increases on "most critical products" agreed with customers, effect 2027 and fully from 2028. Value-based pricing (prices tied to customer productivity gains). About 10% parts increase in Korea. | [1], [28] |
| Concentration and customer power | Four customers about 61% of 2025 sales. TSMC has called High-NA too expensive, and TSMC High-NA volume production is planned for 2030, Samsung's for 2028. | [10], [2], [1] |
| Supplier power | Zeiss is the sole optics supplier; ASML owns a stake accounted as an associate, and in 2016 paid about $1.1bn (Bigdata.com deal data). ASML owns its light-source maker Cymer (acquired 2013). An EUV machine has more than 100,000 parts from about 200 principal suppliers. | Data, [13], [37], [26] |
| Entry and exit | A Chinese state-backed company began producing DUV immersion tools: about 5 in 2026 and 20 in 2027, against ASML's 131 immersion systems in 2025. China's EUV prototype has not yet made a working chip; chip production is targeted for 2028, and 2030 is considered more realistic. | [21], [22], [23] |
| Substitutes | Canon nanoimprint is in production at Kioxia for some memory layers. DUV multi-patterning is a costly workaround. | [31], [24] |
| Regulation | No EUV has ever shipped to China. Advanced DUV immersion needs a license. The MATCH Act would cut DUV immersion sales and servicing to China; CFRA put 10–15% of 2026 sales at risk and less than a 50% chance of enactment. | [8], [19], [20] |
| Technology that could change the structure | High-NA EUV (Intel has exposed more than 1 million wafers; fleet availability approaching 90%). 12-inch masks: pilot line 2031, production 2033. | [1], [35] |
| Source of advantage | Accumulated field data and the supplier ecosystem: "beyond a certain technological threshold, markets no longer correct monopolies." | [36] |
| Profit pool and direction | Litho intensity (lithography content per chip) is rising: DRAM is moving multi-patterning DUV to single-expose EUV, and new DRAM customers are adopting EUV. Gap: no wafer-fab-equipment profit-pool data in Bigdata.com. | [3], [1] |

Duration judgment: for EUV, the advantage should last 15 years or more (judgment). That is longer than the information-technology base rate, where about half of excess returns fade within four to five years (CFROI, a cash-flow return measure, has a 4-year persistence correlation of 0.50; global companies 1983–2015, historical base rate). The exception rests on three pieces of evidence: no rival has accumulated EUV field data, China's EUV effort is years from producing chips, and customers are asking to place orders for 2029–2030 [1].

The DUV business is less protected. Chinese domestic substitution could reach the China DUV revenue within three to five years if export controls tighten (judgment, [24], [38]).

## Earnings quality

| Year | Net income, €bn | Operating cash flow, €bn | Accrual ratio | OCF / net income | Change in deferred revenue, €bn | Stock comp, % of sales | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 5.88 | 10.85 | -16.4% | 1.84 | n/a | 0.63% | derived |
| 2022 | 5.62 | 8.49 | -8.6% | 1.51 | +4.55 | 0.33% | derived |
| 2023 | 7.84 | 5.44 | +6.3% | 0.69 | -1.04 | 0.49% | derived |
| 2024 | 7.57 | 11.17 | -8.1% | 1.47 | +1.13 | 0.61% | derived |
| 2025 | 9.61 | 12.66 | -6.2% | 1.32 | +3.44 | 0.62% | derived |

The accrual ratio is (net income minus operating cash flow) over average total assets. A negative figure means cash came in ahead of reported earnings.

EBITA rebuild for 2025: EBIT €11.30bn plus €0.12bn amortization of intangibles gives EBITA of €11.42bn. FactSet's "operating income after unusual items" differs by only €14m, so no material one-offs were found in 2025 (derived). For Q3 2026, operating profit of €5.16bn (44.4% margin) is clean, but pre-tax margin of 49.3% includes the Mistral gain.

| Flag | Recurrence | Severity | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| €0.5bn Mistral AI fair-value gain in Q3 2026 net income (about €1.3 per share), valued with a venture-capital method (Level 3: no market price, model inputs) | one-off | medium for EPS comparisons | [1], [11] |
| Q2 2026 Technology and IT transformation costs booked mainly in R&D; amount not given | one year | low | [2] |
| Upgrade revenue lifting gross margin (installed-base revenue beat guidance by about €0.4bn in Q3) | recurring but variable | medium | [1], [14] |
| Cash flow depends on down payments: Q3 2026 FCF of €11.4bn "underpinning... down payments"; in 2023 OCF/net income fell to 0.69 as deferred revenue reversed | cyclical | medium | [1] |
| A 2025 cash inflow from receivables factoring (selling receivables early for cash) was questioned at the 2026 AGM. The incentive plan's cash-conversion metric paid 200% of target for 2022–24. Amount not found. | unknown | medium (governance) | [13], [7] |
| Inventory €11.8bn, about 131 days of sales, during a capacity ramp | ramp-related | low | Data |
| Stock compensation 0.6% of sales, expensed under US GAAP | recurring | low | Data |

Piotroski F-score 9 (Q3 2026) and Altman Z of 14.6 (Q2 2026), as reported by FactSet. Free cash flow note: the company's 2025 FCF of €11.0bn [4] matches operating cash flow minus capex (derived). The FactSet free-cash-flow field (€8.5bn) appears to also subtract dividends.

## Capital allocation

| 2021–2025, €bn | Amount | % of OCF | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating cash flow | 48.6 | 100% | reported |
| Capex | 8.2 | 17% | reported |
| Buybacks | 20.7 | 42% | reported |
| Dividends | 11.3 | 23% | reported |
| Acquisitions and net investment purchases (including €1.3bn Mistral) | 0.4 + other investing 2.2 | 5% | reported |
| Cash build (€7.6bn to €13.3bn) | 5.7 | 12% | derived |

- **Buyback return, net of issuance.** Average shares fell from 409.7m (2021) to 388.6m (2025): 21.1m net shares retired for €12.1bn spent in 2022–2025, or about €573 per share. Against €1,419 today that is about 2.5 times, roughly 35–40% a year over an average holding of about 2.8 years. This is above the assumed 9.5% cost of equity. The figure is approximate because average share counts lag the timing of 2021 purchases (derived).
- **2026 buybacks.** €1.1bn in Q2 and €4.1bn in Q3 under the new €12bn 2026–2028 program [2], [1]. The Q1 amount is not in the data. Q3 purchases were made near current prices, so their return is not yet known.
- **Dividend.** €7.50 per share for 2025, up 17% [3]. 2026 interims are €1.88 per quarter [1].
- **Deals.** Five tracked deals totalled $1.46bn disclosed, all cash (Bigdata.com deal data): the Zeiss SMT stake (about $1.1bn, 2016), Mapper (2019) and Berliner Glas (2020–21). Mistral (€1.3bn for about 11%, 2025 [12]) shows a €0.5bn unrealized gain so far, about 38% (derived). Deal premiums and synergy claims are not disclosed.
- **Leverage.** Net cash of about €10.8bn (derived). Rated A1 by Moody's and A+ by Fitch, both stable [17].
- **Incentives.** The short-term bonus is 60% EBIT margin, 20% customer goals and 20% strategic goals. The long-term plan is 30% relative total shareholder return, 30% cash conversion, 20% technology leadership and 20% ESG [7]. No metric rewards return on capital or growth per share. The CEO has said he is tying his pay to employee satisfaction [34].

## What the price implies

| Measure | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Price | €1,419 ($1,589.60 / 1.12) | derived |
| Market cap / EV | €543.6bn / €528.5bn (383.0m shares; net cash €10.8bn; non-operating investments €4.3bn) | derived |
| P/E: FY2026E / FY2027E | 33.6x / 24.3x (EPS €42.3 / €58.4) | derived from consensus |
| EV/EBITDA: trailing / FY2027E | 32.3x / 19.0x | derived |
| Steady-state value (FY2027E NOPAT €21.5bn / 9%) | €239bn, 45% of EV | derived |
| Value attributed to growth beyond 2027 | 55% of EV | derived |
| Warranted P/E (growth 4–5%, return on new investment 40%, cost of equity 9.5%) | 16–19x vs 24.3x actual | derived |

At a 9% cost of capital, the price requires consensus revenue of €58.5bn in 2027 and about €73bn in 2028. Consensus covers only Q1–Q3 2028, so the 2028 figure is an extrapolation (assumed). After that, the price needs 10% annual growth for another 10 years at a 45% EBIT margin, which puts revenue near €190bn in 2038. Alternatives are 8% growth for 14 years or 12% for 8 years. In each case the competitive advantage has to last 10 to 16 years from now (derived).

Base rates, from top-1,000 global companies 1950–2015, inflation-adjusted (historical, not current facts):
- Consensus implies about 31% nominal sales growth a year from 2025 to 2028. Only 4.6% of companies with sales above $25bn grew 20% or more a year in real terms over three years.
- Over ten years, the median real growth for that size class was 1.8% a year. Only 1.5% sustained 15% or more.
- 37% of that class saw real sales fall over three years.

The price therefore assumes growth from a company that is already large, in the top few percent of history.

## Valuation

Assumptions: WACC of 9% (assumed: little debt, an assumed euro risk-free rate of about 3.5%, equity beta 1.2, risk premium 5%; Bigdata.com has no WACC; US 10-year yield is 5.00%). Tax 17% [1]. Incremental invested capital of €0.40 per €1 of new sales (assumed, between 0.22 net of prepayments and 0.71 gross). An explicit forecast for 2027–2041 (15 years, set by the moat judgment). Continuing value with the return on new investment fading to WACC, with a 25% return variant. Valuation date end-2026. ASML is treated as a cyclical: each case includes a demand path, and the bear case includes a downturn.

| Case | Path | Value per share (9%, terminal return = WACC) | With 25% terminal return | Probability | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear | Sales €55bn in 2027–28, -24% to €42bn in 2029 (AI capex digestion plus MATCH Act), then 3–5% growth; EBIT margin 32–40% | €568 | €625 | 30% | judgment |
| Base | €58.5bn 2027, €70bn 2028, -10% in 2029, then 8% fading to 4%; €128bn by 2041; EBIT margin 44% | €1,022 | €1,144 | 50% | judgment |
| Bull | €60bn, €78bn, €88bn, €95bn by 2030, then 11% fading to 5%; €206bn by 2041; EBIT margin 47–48% | €1,619 | €1,834 | 20% | judgment |
| Probability-weighted | | €1,005 | €1,126 | 100% | derived |

Probabilities are anchored on the 37% of large companies with three-year real sales declines and on information technology having the highest operating-margin sensitivity to sales of any sector (0.17; 1950–2015 base rates). The bull case is held below the base case because sustained top-tail growth at this size is rare.

Terminal checks for the base case at 9%:
- Terminal value is 39% of EV.
- The implied terminal EV/EBIT is 9.5x, against 20.4x today.
- ROIC counting prepayments rises from 64% in 2027 to 76% in 2041 (derived), above the 35–43% history. The capital assumption is generous, so the values lean high.

Bridge per share, base case: EV €376.4bn + net cash €10.8bn + investments €4.3bn = equity €391.4bn / 383.0m shares = €1,022. Minority interests are zero, there is no pension deficit in the data, and leases (€61m current) are left out as immaterial.

Base case value per share by WACC and terminal growth (25% terminal return):

| WACC \ g | 2% | 3% | 4% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7% | €1,561 | €1,733 | €2,018 |
| 8% | €1,284 | €1,379 | €1,522 |
| 9% | €1,087 | €1,144 | €1,223 |
| 10% | €941 | €977 | €1,024 |

Comps cross-check (FactSet trailing multiples at each company's last quarter-end, not today's prices):

| Company | P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | ROIC | Operating margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASML (Q3 2026) | 43.5x | 35.3x | 14.5x | 66.6% | 44.4% |

# ASML Holding (ASML): deep dive, 23 Oct 2026

Data as of: share price $1,589.60, the Oct 22, 2026 close in the Bigdata.com company data (about €1,419 at EUR/USD 1.12 on Oct 23); consensus estimates retrieved Oct 23, 2026 (FactSet, quarterly, number of estimates not given); statements FY2025 annual and Q3 2026 quarterly; newest document Oct 23, 2026.

## Summary

ASML is the only company that makes EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines, the tools needed to print the most advanced chips. It also leads the older DUV (deep ultraviolet) segment, and it services an installed base of machines that grows every year. FY2026 sales are guided to €44–45bn, about 36% growth [1].

The economics are exceptional, partly because customers pay large down payments that fund ASML's working capital:
- Return on invested capital (ROIC) was 123% in 2025 on capital net of cash and those prepayments (derived).
- Counting the prepayments as capital, ROIC was 42% (derived), against an assumed 9% cost of capital.

The competitive position rests on a sole-source EUV position that nobody has matched. Nikon left EUV in 2011 [27], and China's EUV prototype has not yet produced a working chip [23]. Pricing power is visible: ASML completed price increases on its most critical products that take effect from 2027 and fully from 2028 [1].

Earnings are mostly clean, with three caveats:
- Q3 2026 net income includes a €0.5bn revaluation gain on the Mistral AI stake [1].
- Gross margin is being lifted by machine-upgrade sales, which the CFO calls a "swing factor" [1].
- Operating cash flow depends on customer down payments, which reversed in 2023.

Capital allocation leans heavily to shareholders: 65% of 2021–2025 operating cash flow went to buybacks and dividends (derived). At today's price, the 2022–2025 buybacks returned roughly 2.5 times their cost (derived, approximate).

At an assumed 9% cost of capital, the price assumes consensus through 2028, then about 10% annual growth for another ten years at a 45% operating margin (derived). The probability-weighted value from three cases is about €1,005 per share at 9% (derived), with a range of €884–1,359 across 8–10% discount rates and terminal assumptions, below the €1,419 price. Peer multiples point the other way, to about €1,900. Most of that gap comes from the discount rate and from how long the advantage is assumed to last.

The main risk is a semiconductor capex cycle that turns after the AI build-out, combined with US legislation (the MATCH Act) that would ban DUV immersion sales and servicing in China. The next dated events are Nov 10, 2026, when the US Affiliates Rule suspension and China's rare-earth export-curb suspension both expire [8], and the Q4 results with 2027 guidance in January–February 2027.

ASML sells lithography systems (EUV, DUV immersion, DUV dry), metrology and inspection tools, and "Installed Base Management": service and upgrades on machines already in customer fabs. ## Economics

ROIC is shown three ways because customer prepayments (€16.0bn of deferred revenue at end-2025) are larger than ASML's whole net operating capital. The report quotes the hand-built ROIC with goodwill and shows the version that counts prepayments as capital beside it.

| Year | Tax rate | NOPAT, €bn | Invested capital, €bn | ROIC (avg capital) | NOPAT margin x turnover | ROIC counting prepayments as capital | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 15.2% | 5.54 | 5.97 | 92.9% (year-end) | 29.8% x 3.12 | 39.9% | derived |
| 2022 | 15.0% | 5.52 | 4.61 | 104.5% | 26.1% x 4.01 | 35.7% | derived |

How the figures are built:
- NOPAT (net operating profit after tax) is EBIT times (1 minus the effective tax rate).
- Invested capital is equity plus debt minus cash and short-term investments minus long-term investments. The operating-side build (assets minus cash and investments, minus non-debt liabilities) gives the same figure.
- Excluding goodwill and intangibles, invested capital is negative in every year, so that version of ROIC has no meaning.
- Return on incremental invested capital (ROIIC) for 2022–2025 was 110% (change in NOPAT over the lagged change in capital, derived).
- The spread over an assumed 9% cost of capital is about 114 points on the quoted basis and about 34 points counting prepayments.
- Reconciliation with FactSet: FactSet's ROIC was 47.4% for FY2025 and 66.6% on a trailing basis at Q3 2026. It divides by total capital (equity plus debt, €24.3bn) without deducting the €13.3bn of cash and €3.8bn of investments.
- R&D is expensed under US GAAP. Capitalizing it would lower every ROIC figure, and the R&D history needed to do that is not in the data.
- Only five years are tabled because the tearsheet returns five fiscal periods and offers no period offset.

Duration judgment: for EUV, the advantage should last 15 years or more (judgment). That is longer than the information-technology base rate, where about half of excess returns fade within four to five years (CFROI, a cash-flow return measure, has a 4-year persistence correlation of 0.50; global companies 1983–2015, historical base rate). The exception rests on three pieces of evidence: no rival has accumulated EUV field data, China's EUV effort is years from producing chips, and customers are asking to place orders for 2029–2030 [1].

The DUV business is less protected. Chinese domestic substitution could reach the China DUV revenue within three to five years if export controls tighten (judgment, [24], [38]).

In each case the competitive advantage has to last 10 to 16 years from now (derived).

Base rates, from top-1,000 global companies 1950–2015, inflation-adjusted (historical, not current facts):
- Consensus implies about 31% nominal sales growth a year from 2025 to 2028. Only 4.6% of companies with sales above $25bn grew 20% or more a year in real terms over three years.
- Over ten years, the median real growth for that size class was 1.8% a year. Only 1.5% sustained 15% or more.
- 37% of that class saw real sales fall over three years.

The price therefore assumes growth from a company that is already large, in the top few percent of history.
